etymologies.etymologyHTML: Borrowed from Dutch noedel (“noodle”)), or from its etymon German Nudel (“piece of pasta, noodle”); further etymology uncertain, probably a variant of Knödel (“dumpling”), from Middle High German knödel (“dumpling; small knot”), and then either:

definitions.definition: (usually in the plural) A string or flat strip of pasta or other dough, usually cooked (at least initially) by boiling, and served in soup or in a dry form mixed with a sauce and other ingredients.

quote.citation: 2003, Ma. Romina M. Gonzalez, Welostit and Other Stories, page 51:
quote.text: One brought two boxes of instant mami noodles.

definitions.definition: (informal) Short for pool noodle (“a long, slender tube or rod, extruded from buoyant foam and usually brightly coloured, used as an exercise tool or toy in swimming pools”).
(by extension) An object which is long and thin like a noodle (sense 1).
(archaic) A dumpling cooked by boiling and served in soup; a knaidel or knödel.
(slang) The penis.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: The origin of the noun is uncertain; it is possibly a variant of noddle (“the head”). The verb is derived from the noun.

definitions.definition: (dated) A person with poor judgment; a fool.

quote.citation: 1751, [Alain-René Lesage], “Which is as Short as the Foregoing”, in [Tobias George Smollett], transl., The Adventures of Gil Blas of Santillane. […], 3rd edition, volume I, London:  […]  J. Osborn, […], →OCLC, book III, page 244:
quote.text: Laura told me the names of all the actors and actreſſes as they preſented themſelves; and, not contented vvith this, the ſatyrical baggage deſcrib'd their characters nicely, as they appeared. "This here (ſaid ſhe) is a noodle—That fellovv is a brute: […]."

quote.citation: 1796 March 25 (first performance), J[ames] C. Cross, “The Village Doctor, a Burletta. […]”, in Parnassian Bagatelles: Being a Miscellaneous Collection of Poetical Attempts. […], London:  […]  Burton and Co. […]; [for] Bellamy, […], published 1796, →OCLC, page 140:
quote.text: You vvrong me, noodle (boxes his ears). Novv then to the point.

quote.citation: 1826, [Walter Scott], chapter III, in Woodstock; Or, The Cavalier. […], volume I, Edinburgh:  […]  [James Ballantyne and Co.] for Archibald Constable and Co.; London: Longman, Rees, Orme, Brown, and Green, →OCLC, page 67:
quote.text: [T]hou would'st fling thy cuckoldy steeple-hat one way, and that bloodthirsty long-sword another, and trip like the noodles of Hogs-Norton, when the pigs play on the organ.

quote.citation: 1839, Sydney Smith, “Preface”, in The Works of the Rev. Sydney Smith. […], volume I, London:  […]  [A[ndrew] Spottiswoode] for Longman, Orme, Brown, Green, and Longmans, […], →OCLC, page viii:
quote.text: [A] long and hopeless career in your profession, the chuckling grin of noodles, the sarcastic leer of the genuine political rogue—  […]  these were the penalties exacted for liberality of opinion at that period; and not only was there no pay, but there were many stripes.

quote.citation: 1854, Charles Dickens, “Final”, in Hard Times. For These Times, London: Bradbury & Evans, […], →OCLC, book the third (Garnering), page 349:
quote.text: If that portrait could speak, sir,—  […]  it would testify, that a long period has elapsed since I first habitually addressed it as the picture of a Noodle. Nothing that a Noodle does, can awaken surprise or indignation; the proceedings of a Noodle can only inspire contempt.

quote.citation: 1905 February 4, Alfred Colbeck, “Netted: The Story of a Capture”, in The Boy’s Own Paper, volume XXVII, number 19 (number 1360 overall), London: “Boy’s Own Paper” Office, […], →OCLC, chapter V (A Surprising Capture), page 314, column 1:
quote.text: "What are you two noodleth laughing at?" Norrie went on, with a touch of indignation. "Ithn't the thenthe of thent in hith nothe?"The speaker is lisping.

definitions.definition: (slang) The brain; the head.

quote.citation: 2006, Mark Victor Hansen, Art Linkletter, “Mind or Are You ‘Sageing’ or Aging?”, in How to Make the Rest of Your Life the Best of Your Life, Nashville, Tenn.: Nelson Books, Thomas Nelson, →ISBN, page 172:
quote.text: [W]hat appears to at first glance to be a thinking problem can be a problem with sight or hearing.  […]  There's nothing wrong with your noodle; it's your sensory equipment that needs a bit of help. Learn to compensate.

definitions.definition: (transitive, obsolete) To fool or trick (someone).
(intransitive, British, dialectal, informal) To engage in frivolous behaviour; to fool around or waste time.
(transitive, intransitive, Shetland, singing) To hum or sing (a tune) at a low pitch or volume.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: The origin of the verb is uncertain; it is possibly derived:

definitions.definition: (chiefly jazz) To play (a musical instrument or passage of music) or to sing (a passage of music) in an improvisatory or lighthearted manner; also, to play (a series of ornamental notes) on an instrument.
(US, informal) To ponder or think about (something).
(transitive)
(chiefly jazz) To play a musical instrument or to sing in an improvisatory or lighthearted manner; also, to play a series of ornamental notes on an instrument.

quote.citation: 1965, W[ystan] H[ugh] Auden, “Thanksgiving for a Habitat. The Cave of Nakedness (for Louis and Emmie Kronenberger).”, in About the House, New York, N.Y.; Toronto, Ont.: Random House, →OCLC, page 34:
quote.text: [A]udible here and there / in the half-dark, members of an avian orchestra / are already softly noodling, limbering up for / an overture at sunrise,  […]

quote.citation: 2020 November 9, Gwen Ihnat, “With McCartney III, Paul McCartney Offers Lessons from a Legendary Life”, in The A.V. Club‎[2], archived from the original on 16 May 2022:
quote.text: We’ve learned the prospective danger of Macca [Paul McCartney] noodling around in the studio from McCartney III’s predecessors—“Wonderful Christmastime” came out of the McCartney II sessions, after all.

definitions.definition: To ponder or think, especially in an unproductive or unsystematic manner; to muse.
To attempt in an informal or uncertain manner; to fiddle.
Often followed by about or around: to mess around, to play.
(US, informal)
(intransitive)
(chiefly jazz) An improvised passage of music played on an instrument; also, a series of ornamental notes played on an instrument; a trill.
To search (mullock (“mining or ore processing waste”)) for opals.
To obtain (an opal) by searching through mullock.
(also figuratively) To clear extraneous material from (an opal).
(transitive)
(intransitive) To search mullock for opals; to fossick.

quote.citation: 1989, Association for Industrial Archaeology, Industrial archaeology review, volume 12:
quote.text: On the Olympic Field the tour-group is permitted to ‘noodle’ (hunt for opals) on the waste or mullock heaps  […]

quote.citation: 1994, RonMoon, Outback Australia: a Lonely Planet Australia guide:
quote.text: In Coober Pedy, noodling for opals is generally discouraged, although a few tourist spots, such as the Old Timers Mine, have noodle pits open to the public.

quote.citation: 2006, Making Waves: 10 Years of the Byron Bay Writers Festival, edited by Marele Day, Susan Bradley Smith, and Fay Knight, (Please provide the book title or journal name):
quote.text: We learn how Lennon used to noodle (fossick) for opal as a kid, how camels were for a long time the only form of transportation, and where the name 'Coober Pedy' came from.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: Unknown; perhaps related to guddle (“to catch (fish) with the hands”).

definitions.definition: (transitive, fishing) To catch (fish (usually very large catfish), turtles, or other aquatic animals) with the hands; also, to catch (fish) using a gaff or fishing spear; to gaff.
